results.name: lag1_response_autocorrelation
results.description: Pearson correlation between a response and the same participant's immediately preceding response (consecutive trial_index); observed above the null means people show sequential yes/no carryover (perseveration) the trial-independent model fails to produce, below means alternation it fails to produce.

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate in the second half of each session (trial_index >= 225) minus the first half; a positive/negative observed value beyond the null means people drift toward more/fewer yeses over the session, a drift the stationary model does not produce.

results.name: far_rule_extrapolation_yes_rate
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples share a common divisor >= 2, yes-rate for non-example targets divisible by that divisor lying more than 10 beyond the examples' range; observed above the null means people extrapolate rules farther outside the examples' span than the model predicts, below means they confine rules to the examples' range more than the model does.
results.code:
# name: far_rule_extrapolation_yes_rate
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples share a common divisor >= 2, yes-rate for non-example targets divisible by that divisor lying more than 10 beyond the examples' range; observed above the null means people extrapolate rules farther outside the examples' span than the model predicts, below means they confine rules to the examples' range more than the model does.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(exi, axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(np.int64).to_numpy()
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = (k >= 2) & (g >= 2) & (t % np.maximum(g, 1) == 0) & ((t < lo - 10) | (t > hi + 10)) & ~is_ex
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: nearest_first_minus_nearest_last
results.description: For sets of 3-4 examples, yes-rate for non-example targets whose nearest example is the first one shown minus that for targets whose nearest example is the last one shown; observed above the null means people show stronger primacy than the anchoring model produces, below means weaker primacy or a recency advantage the model misses.
results.code:
# name: nearest_first_minus_nearest_last
# description: For sets of 3-4 examples, yes-rate for non-example targets whose nearest example is the first one shown minus that for targets whose nearest example is the last one shown; observed above the null means people show stronger primacy than the anchoring model produces, below means weaker primacy or a recency advantage the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    nearest = np.argmin(d, axis=1)
    dmin = d.min(axis=1)
    # unique nearest only (no ties)
    ties = (d == dmin[:, None]).sum(axis=1) > 1
    base = (k >= 3) & (dmin > 0) & ~ties
    first = base & (nearest == 0)
    last = base & (nearest == k - 1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if first.sum() == 0 or last.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[first].mean() - r[last].mean())

results.name: ruleless_inside_minus_outside_range
results.description: Among multi-example sets with no common divisor (gcd = 1), yes-rate for non-example targets inside the examples' [min, max] range minus that for targets outside it; observed above the null means people's range-based (similarity) generalization is stronger/sharper-edged than the model predicts, below means weaker.
results.code:
# name: ruleless_inside_minus_outside_range
# description: Among multi-example sets with no common divisor (gcd = 1), yes-rate for non-example targets inside the examples' [min, max] range minus that for targets outside it; observed above the null means people's range-based (similarity) generalization is stronger/sharper-edged than the model predicts, below means weaker.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(exi, axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    base = (k >= 2) & (g == 1) & ~is_ex
    inside = base & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    outside = base & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: single_example_near_minus_far
results.description: For single-example sets, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example) minus yes-rate for targets more than 30 away; observed above the null means people's generalization from one number is more sharply local than the model predicts, below means it is flatter (broader) than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: single_example_near_minus_far
# description: For single-example sets, yes-rate for targets within 10 of the example (excluding the example) minus yes-rate for targets more than 30 away; observed above the null means people's generalization from one number is more sharply local than the model predicts, below means it is flatter (broader) than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ns = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~ns.str.contains(",")
    e = pd.to_numeric(ns.where(single, "nan"), errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(t - e)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    s = single.to_numpy()
    near = s & (dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)
    far = s & (dist > 30)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: in_range_rule_violation_yes_rate
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples share a common divisor >= 2, yes-rate for targets inside the examples' [min, max] range that are NOT divisible by that divisor; observed above the null means people generalize by numeric proximity (ranges) over a clear rule more than the model does, below means the model over-weights ranges against rules.
results.code:
# name: in_range_rule_violation_yes_rate
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples share a common divisor >= 2, yes-rate for targets inside the examples' [min, max] range that are NOT divisible by that divisor; observed above the null means people generalize by numeric proximity (ranges) over a clear rule more than the model does, below means the model over-weights ranges against rules.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(exi, axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(np.int64).to_numpy()
    m = (k >= 2) & (g >= 2) & (t % np.maximum(g, 1) != 0) & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed above the model's null means the model under-produces yeses to the examples (its noise/gain/bias leak too much belief away from seen numbers), below means it over-produces them.
